lessons.title: Exponential growth over time (Extended)
lessons.summary: Model a fixed percentage increase per time period and forecast a future amount using a power of the growth factor.
lessons.objective: Model a fixed percentage increase per time period and forecast a future amount using a power of the growth factor.
lessons.before: Find a percentage multiplier and identify a complete time interval. The exponent counts elapsed intervals, starting at zero.
lessons.ideas:
From initial value \(A_0\), the model after \(k\) complete periods is \(A_k=A_0m^k\). For an increase of \(r\%\) per period, use \(m=1+\frac{r}{100}\).

At \(k=0\), the factor is \(m^0=1\), so the value is the initial amount. An example is \(10\times1.5^k\), where each period has a \(50\%\) increase.

Subtract the dates to count elapsed years when comparing matching points in the year. For an increase in amount, subtract the initial amount from the modelled final amount.
lessons.method:
Why does a multiplier become a power?

A forecast may say that a quantity grows by a fixed percentage per year, per week or per other interval. Apply the percentage to the latest amount at the start of that interval.

What do the three parts of the equation tell me?

The number outside the power gives the initial value. The base gives the change per period. The exponent says how many times that change has happened.

How do I read the date and answer the quantity asked for?

The starting date is period zero. A question may ask for the complete forecast at a later date, or only the increase from the starting amount.
mistakes: Adding the same amount each period is a different model. In exponential growth the same factor acts on a growing quantity.
The exponent applies to the multiplier. If you put the initial amount and the multiplier in the brackets before taking a power, you also raise the initial amount.
Rounding the amount after each year changes the next year’s base and can shift the final answer.

examples.title: Forecast a population several years ahead
examples.question: A town has \(3600\) residents at the beginning of the model. The population is modelled to grow by \(1.6\%\) each year. Estimate the population at the end of \(2\) years. Give your answer to the nearest hundred.
examples.solution:
One year uses the multiplier \(1.016\).

\(3600\times1.016^{2}\approx3716.12\) before the final rounding.

To the nearest hundred, this is \(3700\) residents.

examples.title: Read the growth rate from the factor
examples.question: The forecast for a settlement is \(P(k)=6240\times1.032^k\), where \(k\) counts years since the start. Find the annual percentage increase in the model.
examples.solution:
The factor multiplying the population each year is \(1.032\).

The part in excess of 1 is \(1.032-1=0.032\).

The increase per year is \(3.2\%\).

examples.title: Find the additional amount over several periods
examples.question: Moisture in a prepared sample has starting mass \(980\) g. For this test the model increases the mass by \(5.5\%\) each day. By how many grams does the modelled mass increase over \(2\) days? Give the exact increase.
examples.solution:
Compute the final mass. \(980\times1.055^{2}=1090.7645\) g.

Subtract the starting mass to find the increase.

\(1090.7645-980=110.7645\) g.

lessons.title: Exponential decay and depreciation (Extended)
lessons.summary: Apply a retained fraction repeatedly, distinguish the amount remaining from the amount lost and model depreciation.
lessons.objective: Apply a retained fraction repeatedly, distinguish the amount remaining from the amount lost and model depreciation.
lessons.before: On a reduction of r percent, the share retained is 100 minus r percent. One multiplier describes that retained share.
lessons.ideas:
For a loss of \(r\%\) per period, use \(m=1-\frac{r}{100}\), with \(0<m<1\). Halving means applying \(\frac12\) once per specified interval.

\(\text{amount lost}=\text{initial amount}-\text{amount remaining}\). The fraction still left after \(k\) periods is \(m^k\).

Multiply the original value by the annual retaining factor raised to the number of years. From a given model such as \(V_k=900(0.92)^k\), read an annual decrease of \(8\%\).
lessons.method:
What part survives each period?

In an exponential decay model, the amount gets smaller by the same proportion in equal intervals. A later decline starts from the new, smaller amount.

Am I finding the amount left or the amount lost?

The model equation produces the amount remaining at a later time. Other questions use that result to ask for a difference or a percentage.

How do I use the same model for the value of an item?

An item that loses the same percentage of its current value each year follows an exponential depreciation model.
mistakes: For a loss of \(18\%\), a multiplier of \(0.18\) would keep only \(18\%\). The model needs the multiplier \(0.82\).
Multiplying the loss rate by the number of periods ignores the fact that each loss acts on a different amount.
The annual percentage loss can stay the same while the amount lost in pounds becomes smaller.

examples.title: Find the amount remaining after repeated loss
examples.question: A pigment has initial mass \(100\) mg. It loses \(8\%\) of its remaining mass in each treatment. Find the exact mass remaining after \(2\) treatments.
examples.solution:
One treatment retains \(92\%\). Use multiplier \(0.92\).

Apply it once per treatment. The remaining mass is \(100\times0.92^{2}=84.64\) mg.

\(100\times0.92^{2}=84.64\) mg remains.

examples.title: Find the amount lost in total
examples.question: A pigment has initial mass \(320\) mg. It loses \(12\%\) of its remaining mass in each treatment. How many milligrams are lost over \(2\) treatments? Give the exact amount.
examples.solution:
One treatment retains \(88\%\). Use multiplier \(0.88\).

Apply it once per treatment. The remaining mass is \(320\times0.88^{2}=247.808\) mg.

The total loss is \(320-247.808=72.192\) mg.

examples.title: Model annual depreciation
examples.question: A new cutting machine is valued at £8350. It loses \(18\%\) of its value each year. Estimate its value after \(2\) years, to the nearest pound.
examples.solution:
It retains \(82\%\) of its value from one year to the next.

\(8350\times0.82^{2}\approx5615\) to the nearest pound.

The estimated value is £5615.

lessons.title: Finding an exponential model from data (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use consecutive readings to recover a per-period multiplier, work back to an initial value and compare additive and exponential forecasts.
lessons.objective: Use consecutive readings to recover a per-period multiplier, work back to an initial value and compare additive and exponential forecasts.
lessons.before: Use the model equation after one or more time intervals and be comfortable dividing by a decimal factor.
lessons.ideas:
Divide one reading by the reading one period before it. Check the same ratio with another pair where data are supplied.

\(A_k=A_0m^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A_0=\frac{A_k}{m^k}\). Check the recovered value with the original forward model.

Convert factor to rate by comparing it with 1. For a factor above 1, the extra part is growth. For a factor below 1, the missing part is decay.
lessons.method:
How can a table reveal the multiplier?

With equally spaced measurements, use a ratio to test for a constant factor. Use a difference to test for an additive model.

How do I recover the amount at time zero?

A later reading has already had the multiplier applied once per completed period. The same equation can run backwards if the factor is positive.

How are rate, factor and fixed change different?

An exponential predictor keeps its multiplier. An additive predictor keeps its change in units. You can compare two results at the same time.
mistakes: A constant ratio may have increasing differences. Subtracting two readings gives a change in units and does not recover the multiplying factor.
Dividing by \(m\) just once undoes one period, even when the question gives a value many periods later.
Two models can agree at the first step and then separate. Matching the first change does not make the forecasts identical.

examples.title: Recover the multiplier from paired readings
examples.question:
The table gives three readings at equal intervals. Each reading is multiplied by the same number to get the next one. Find that multiplier.

Elapsed intervalsReading
\(0\)\(125\)
\(1\)\(135\)
\(2\)\(145.8\)
examples.solution:
Divide a later reading by the immediately preceding reading.

\(\frac{135}{125}=1.08\).

The next pair confirms the same factor. \(\frac{145.8}{135}=1.08\).

examples.title: Recover the initial value from a later reading
examples.question: The model for a measure multiplies its value by \(1.16\) every hour. At the end of \(2\) hours its value is \(908.28\) units. What was the value at the start, measured in units?
examples.solution:
The original value was multiplied by \(1.16^{2}\).

Undo that factor. \(\frac{908.28}{1.16^{2}}=675\) units.

Substituting the original into the forward model recovers \(908.28\) units.

examples.title: Infer a rate from two consecutive readings
examples.question: Under an exponential model, a reading is \(784\) at the end of hour \(2\) and \(627.2\) at the end of hour \(3\). Find the percentage decrease per hour.
examples.solution:
Divide the later reading by the earlier one to find one hour’s multiplier.

\(\frac{627.2}{784}=0.8\).

Its difference from 1 gives the fractional change. The decrease is \(20\%\).

lessons.title: Time to reach a growth or decay target (Extended)
lessons.summary: Check successive whole periods and use the exact inequality to find the first time a growth or decay target is met.
lessons.objective: Check successive whole periods and use the exact inequality to find the first time a growth or decay target is met.
lessons.before: Know how to evaluate the exponential model after a whole number of periods. Read the language used for inclusive limits.
lessons.ideas:
A growth model with factor above 1 is increasing. If the current reading passes the target and the preceding reading fails, this is the first successful period.

‘At most’ allows equality and uses \(\le\). ‘Strictly below’ excludes equality and uses \(<\). Use unrounded model values near a boundary.

First find the number of full intervals. Multiply the winning interval count by the number of days, weeks or hours in one interval, as requested.
lessons.method:
When does a growing amount first reach a target?

Write down the starting amount, factor and comparison. Evaluate the model at successive whole periods until the condition first holds.

When does a falling amount first go low enough?

For a falling amount, the readings are decreasing. A lower limit may use an inclusive comparison or a strict one.

What if the period is different from the requested unit?

Sometimes a model factor applies per week or every three hours. Successive model values are checked only at the specified completed intervals.
mistakes: Showing only a successful value leaves open whether an earlier value already worked.
A value equal to the cutoff is the first successful one only when the instruction includes equality.
Do not substitute the elapsed hours as an exponent when one multiplier applies to a block of three hours.

examples.title: Find the first whole-period threshold
examples.question: A reading starts at \(150\) units. In the model it rises by \(12\%\) each day. Find the first whole number of days after which the reading is strictly above \(200\) units.
examples.solution:
Each interval multiplies the reading by \(1.12\). Work forwards until the condition is first true.

Completed intervalsReadingCompare with target
\(2\)\(188.16\)\(188.16\le200\)
\(3\)\(210.7392\)\(210.7392>200\)

So the first possible time is \(3\) days.

examples.title: Find the first whole-period threshold
examples.question: A reading starts at \(590\) units. In the model it falls by \(18\%\) each day. Find the first whole number of days after which the reading is strictly below \(396.716\) units.
examples.solution:

Completed intervalsReadingCompare with target

\(3\)\(325.30712\)\(325.30712<396.716\)

So the first possible time is \(3\) days.

examples.title: Find the first whole-period threshold
